title: Tamil Playback Singer Krishnaraj Dies at 75 in Chennai, Days After Composer Deva
excerpt: The voice of 'Thanjavooru Mannu Eduthu' and 'Vellarikka Pinju Vellarikka' sang more than 300 songs; Chief Minister Vijay and Sarath Kumar led tributes to Deva's frequent collaborator.
body:
• Tamil playback singer Krishnaraj Ramasamy died in Chennai on Thursday, October 22, at age 75; the cause had not been confirmed, with reports citing ill health.
  • He sang more than 300 Tamil film songs and won the Tamil Nadu State Government Award for Best Playback Singer for 'Thanjavooru Mannu Eduthu' in Porkkaalam (1997).
  • His death came five days after his frequent collaborator, composer Deva, died on October 17; Deva's nephew, actor Karthik Sabesh, died on October 20.
  • Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay and actor R. Sarath Kumar led tributes; his remains were kept at his Valasaravakkam residence in Chennai before final rites in his hometown, Vembadithalam in Salem district.

Tamil playback singer Krishnaraj Ramasamy died in Chennai on Thursday, October 22, at the age of 75. Cinema Express reported he had sung more than 300 songs in Tamil films, including Paruthiveeran, Arunachalam and Kadhal Kottai, and that the reason for his death was not yet known. ANI's report, carried by NewKerala, said he died due to ill health and that his remains were kept at his residence in Valasaravakkam, Chennai, for the public and film fraternity to pay respects, before final rites in his hometown of Vembadithalam in Salem district.

"I was shocked and deeply saddened to hear the news of the passing of Mr. Krishnaraj, the renowned playback singer of Tamil cinema. With his unique voice and songs brimming with enthusiasm, playback singer Mr Krishnaraj had captivated the hearts of his fans. His demise is a great loss to Tamil cinema."

— C. Joseph Vijay, Tamil Nadu Chief Minister

A voice built with composer Deva

Krishnaraj's career was tied to composer Deva, who died on October 17, five days earlier. Deva recorded Krishnaraj's first film song for Adhikaalai Subavelai, a film that was never released in theatres. Through the 1990s the pair produced the songs listeners still name first: 'Vellarikka Pinju Vellarikka' from Kadhal Kottai (1996), and 'Kaathadikkuthu Kaathadikkuthu' and 'Tirupathi Ezhumalai Venkatesa' from Ninaivirukkum Varai, as Cinema Express listed.

His signature recording was 'Thanjavooru Mannu Eduthu' from Porkkaalam (1997), composed by Deva, which won him the Tamil Nadu State Government Award for Best Playback Singer. Cinema Express reported the track was played at the 2016 funeral of Sellapan Ramanathan, the President of Singapore who hailed from Tamil Nadu — a measure of how far a Tamil film song travelled with the diaspora.

Tributes from the industry

Actor R. Sarath Kumar listed the Krishnaraj songs from his own films, as Live Mint reported: 'Paasamulla Sooriyane' from Vinnukkum Mannukkum, 'Thaayae Thirisoolee' from Simmarasie, 'Sokku Sundari' from Moovendar, 'Karuda Karuda' from Natpukaga, the sorrowful song from Meesaikkaara Nanban, and 'Naalu Vaarthai Pesalaiae' from Periya Kaaval Thozhil. He wrote that through the richness of his voice and his emotionally charged renditions, Krishnaraj would forever live in the hearts of music lovers, and called his passing an irreplaceable loss to the world of music.

Singer Chinmayi Sripaada wrote, "Oh God. This is a really tough week." Singer Sujatha Mohan said she was heartbroken, calling Krishnaraj Deva's favourite singer and her own, and noting he had supervised many of Deva's songs she sang. Singer Anuradha Sriram visited his Chennai home to pay tribute, Live Mint reported.

Context and what's next

The week has compounded Tamil cinema's losses: Deva on October 17, his nephew actor Karthik Sabesh on October 20, and now Krishnaraj on October 22. No cause of death has been officially confirmed for Krishnaraj, and reports differ only in phrasing — 'not yet known' and 'ill health' — not on the central facts of age, place and date. Final rites were expected in Vembadithalam, Salem district, after public homage in Chennai. What remains is the catalogue: more than 300 songs, an award-winning signature track, and a folk-energy voice that defined Deva-era Tamil film music for a generation of listeners in Tamil Nadu and abroad.
